blocks.text: As a fluid moves through a pipe of varying cross-section and height, the pressure changes along the pipe. Bernoulli's equation is the fundamental equation of fluid dynamics that relates pressure to fluid speed and height. In deriving it we assume that the fluid is incompressible, non-viscous and flows in a steady-state manner. Consider the flow of the fluid through the pipe in time t (Fig. 5.16).

The force on the upper end of the fluid is P1 A1, where P1 is the pressure and A1 the area of cross-section at the upper end. The work done on the fluid by the fluid behind it in moving it through a distance delta x1 is W1 = F1 delta x1 = P1 A1 delta x1. Similarly the work done on the fluid at the lower end is W2 = -F2 delta x2 = -P2 A2 delta x2, where P2 is the pressure, A2 the area of cross-section of the lower end and delta x2 the distance moved by the fluid in the same time interval t; W2 is taken negative because this work is done against the fluid force. The work done is W = W1 + W2, or W = P1 A1 delta x1 - P2 A2 delta x2 ... (5.19). If v1 and v2 are the velocities at the upper and lower ends, W = P1 A1 v1 t - P2 A2 v2 t. From the equation of continuity (Eq. 5.18) A1 v1 = A2 v2, hence A1 v1 t = A2 v2 t = V (volume), so W = (P1 - P2) V ... (5.20). If m is the mass and rho the density, V = m / rho, so Eq. 5.20 becomes W = (P1 - P2) m / rho ... (5.21).

A part of this work is utilised by the fluid in changing its kinetic energy and a part in changing its gravitational potential energy: change in KE, delta KE = (1/2) m v2^2 - (1/2) m v1^2 ... (5.22); change in PE, delta PE = m g h2 - m g h1 ... (5.23), where h1 and h2 are the heights of the upper and lower ends. Applying the law of conservation of energy to this volume of fluid, (P1 - P2) m / rho = (1/2) m v2^2 - (1/2) m v1^2 + m g h2 - m g h1 ... (5.24). Rearranging Eq. 5.24, P1 + (1/2) rho v1^2 + rho g h1 = P2 + (1/2) rho v2^2 + rho g h2.

blocks.title: Bernoulli's equation
blocks.text: P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant. The sum of the pressure, the kinetic energy per unit volume and the potential energy per unit volume is the same at every point of a steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow.

blocks.long_description: The net work done on a slug of incompressible fluid by the pressures at its two ends equals the pressure difference times its volume, and by conservation of energy this goes into its change of kinetic and gravitational potential energy, which gives Bernoulli's equation: pressure plus half the density times speed squared plus density times g times height is constant along the flow. Where streamlines crowd and the speed rises the pressure falls, which lifts an aeroplane wing, swings a spinning ball, draws air into a filter pump and petrol into a carburetor, lifts paint in a sprayer, lets a Venturi meter measure speed from a pressure drop, and makes liquid leave a tank orifice at the speed of free fall through the depth. A sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid feels a drag proportional to its radius, speed and the viscosity, so a falling droplet speeds up until drag balances weight at a terminal velocity proportional to the square of its radius. Real fluids all have viscosity; a superfluid has none and can creep over the walls of its container.
